cleanParagraphs: After the storm, Noah and Ms. Rivera arrived at the community planetarium to prepare for the evening event. The control-room door remained locked, and the main power was off. Instead of forcing the door, Noah checked the old duty records. He carefully examined each page and found a note about a spare key.

The note directed them to a locked drawer near the front desk. Ms. Rivera called Dr. Hall, who confirmed the safe entry procedure. Noah collected the spare key, and they entered the control room together. Inside, they noticed water around a soaked fuse box, so they stopped and recorded the damage before touching anything.

After the fuse box dried, the console received power again. Its lights flashed, but the dome stayed still. Noah watched the voltage display and said, “Look—the reading is changing right now, and the warning light is blinking now.” Ms. Rivera replied, “The system normally needs a steady voltage before the dome motor starts.”

They compared the live readings with the operating guide. Noah pointed to the cooling unit. “The fan usually runs whenever the console operates, but it is not turning at the moment.” Ms. Rivera agreed that the heat could damage the system. They paused the test and marked the unusual signal. “Right now, we are choosing to repair the fan instead of forcing the dome open.”

Mina arrived with drying cloths, a small blower, and safe electrical tools. Following the recorded steps, the three cleaned the wet fuse box and reconnected the cooling fan. When the fan began turning, Noah reported, “So far, we have removed the water, and Mina has secured the loose cable. The console has shown a stable reading for several minutes.”

Noah continued, “We have cleared the warning light, but we have not checked the dome sensor yet.” Ms. Rivera studied these latest results rather than guessing. “The repairs have made the main system safer,” she said. “So far, we have gathered enough evidence for a low-power test, but the sensor remains an unresolved issue.” They recorded every repair and prepared the testing area.

Through a video call, Dr. Hall explained the safety requirements without doing the work for them. “Before testing, you have to clear the entire dome track,” he said. “Everyone must stand behind the yellow line, and Noah has to confirm the emergency stop button.” The team understood that these checks had to be completed before any movement.

Mina inspected one side of the track while Noah checked the other. Ms. Rivera noticed a maintenance ladder beside the rail. “We must pause the test,” Noah said. “The ladder has to be moved first.” Together, the students carried it to the storage room and checked the track again. Before they could begin the low-power safety test, they had to check the track one final time.

Before the final test, Noah compared their practical plan with a less likely situation. “If the sensor passes, we will open the planetarium as planned,” he said. “If it fails again tonight, we will hold a small star-map lesson instead. If we had more repair time, we would examine every wire, but visitors are arriving soon.”

Ms. Rivera kept the star maps ready. The team started the test behind the yellow line. The sensor reading stayed steady, and the dome opened smoothly. “If we ignored the evidence, we would risk the equipment,” Noah said. Their result showed that if a team follows every safety step, it reduces the risk. They welcomed visitors on time. If the sensor failed later, they would use the star-map lesson as their backup plan.

mainIdea.text: After a storm stopped the community planetarium's control system, Noah, Ms. Rivera, Mina, and Dr. Hall used evidence to solve the problem safely. They checked old records before entering the locked control room, observed live voltage readings, and compared the console's behavior with its normal operating rules. Mina helped Noah dry the fuse box and reconnect the cooling fan, while Noah reported which repairs had been completed and which issue remained. The team did not force the dome or skip required checks. They cleared the track, confirmed the emergency stop button, and removed a ladder that created danger. Noah also prepared realistic and alternative plans for the event. When the sensor passed, the dome opened safely, visitors entered on time, and the star-map lesson remained available as a backup.
